# The Hours We Misplaced

The office was between a shoe repair shop and a place that sold lampshades. Its sign read **MUNICIPAL TIME RECOVERY**, though most people assumed it meant parking tickets. The windows were frosted, the door stuck in damp weather, and inside, behind a counter with a brass bell, Leena kept three clocks. They never agreed.

This was not a fault. The clock above the door showed the time outside. The one on Leena’s desk showed the time available for return. The third, a little travel clock with a cracked leather case, had belonged to her father and no longer moved at all. It displayed 4:17.

People came in because they had lost an hour.

They described it in different ways. A man would say he had sat down after lunch and looked up to find it dark. A woman would say the train journey home had vanished from her memory, although she had arrived with her bags and bought milk on the way. Children were more precise. They knew exactly when an hour had gone missing, and they were usually angry about it.

Leena asked for a date, an approximate time, and a description of the circumstances. Then she checked the ledger.

Most missing hours could be found. They gathered in the places where people stopped paying attention: hospital corridors, queues, airport lounges, kitchens during arguments. The office had been built to collect and hold them until their owners came looking.

On Tuesday morning, a man in a yellow raincoat asked for the hour he had spent waiting to learn whether his daughter had been born safely.

“She’s twenty-six now,” he said. “I don’t know why I thought of it today.”

“Is it lost?”

“I remember the chairs. The vending machine. I remember being frightened.” He folded his raincoat over one arm. “But when I try to remember what I did for that whole hour, there’s nothing.”

Leena found it under October, twenty-six years earlier. It had been stored in a small blue envelope, the kind used for airmail. She opened the flap and listened. Each hour made a sound if you held it close enough. This one contained shoes crossing a polished floor, a can falling into a vending-machine tray, and a young man whispering, “Come on,” to no one in particular.

“It’s here,” she said.

The man leaned toward the counter. “Can I have it back?”

“Of course. But I should tell you how it works.”

She had given the explanation thousands of times. An hour could be returned only once. It would not send him into the past or let him make a different choice. At some point in the next few days, he would find an ordinary hour of his life opening unexpectedly wide. Within it, he would remember what had been missing.

“That sounds all right,” he said.

“It can be difficult.”

He considered this. “She was born safely?”

“Yes.”

“I know. I called her last night.” He smiled with some embarrassment. “Go ahead.”

Leena gave him the envelope. He put it in his coat pocket with surprising care.

For most of her career, she had liked that part of the job. Someone arrived unsettled by a gap in their life, and she could tell them the hour had not been thrown away. It was still theirs.

The rest of the job was filing.

At noon she ate a pear over the sink in the back room. Then she opened a letter from the city council. Its language was plain. The office would close at the end of the month. Recent studies showed that recovered hours produced no measurable increase in wellbeing. Fewer people had applied each year. The building needed electrical work, and the shoe repair shop next door had asked about expanding.

Leena read the letter twice. There was a number to call if she had questions. She placed it beside the desk clock and served the next visitor, who wanted forty minutes from a school assembly in 1988.

By closing time she had decided not to call. She would begin with the storage cabinets. There were eleven of them, each as tall as the door, and an index that reached back eighty-three years. She did not know what the council intended to do with the hours, but she knew they would want a count.

The first cabinet held the oldest. Some of the envelopes had grown thin and soft. Their labels had been written by clerks who were long dead, in scripts Leena recognized as readily as faces. Mr. Vale pressed too hard with his pen. A woman named S. Rahman wrote her sevens with a line through them. The former chief clerk, whose name Leena had never learned, noted weather in the margins.

*October 3. Thick fog all morning.*

*June 18. Terrible heat.*

She counted until her eyes hurt. At the back of the third shelf, beneath a box of rubber bands, she found an envelope without a label. The paper was yellow and folded at one corner.

Leena held it to her ear. A screen door slammed. A spoon struck the rim of a cup. Someone was whistling badly, stopping and starting.

She knew the tune. Her father used to whistle it while he made tea. He never got past the first line.

She took the envelope to her desk and examined it under the lamp. In the lower right corner, almost erased by time, were her initials. She had written them at sixteen, when the office let children leave an hour for safekeeping.

She remembered the visit. Her father had brought her after school, telling her that the service was free and she might be glad of it one day. At the counter she had rolled her eyes. They had argued on the bus over whether she could travel alone to a concert in another city. At sixteen, she had thought he was keeping her life small on purpose. She had chosen an hour at random—or so she had believed—and made him wait outside while the clerk put it away.

Her father had died nine years ago. The hour had remained in the cabinet through the years Leena worked here, close enough to find whenever she had wanted to look for it.

She took it home.

Her apartment was on the fourth floor of a building with unreliable heating. The little travel clock stood on the kitchen shelf, still at 4:17. She did not remember when it had stopped. Her father had kept winding it long after he no longer traveled, and she had kept it without trying to make it run.

The envelope lay on the table while she cooked rice, washed the pan, and called her brother. She told him about the closure, but not about the hour.

“They’ll offer you something else,” he said.

“Maybe.”

“You could come here for a while.”

He lived by the sea, in a house full of children and wet shoes. Leena loved visiting him and was always relieved to leave. She said she would think about it.

After they hung up, she sat at the table and opened the envelope. There was nothing inside that she could see. The opening was enough; the hour knew where to go.

It arrived two days later while she was buying oranges.

She had gone to the market before work. Rain tapped on the canvas roofs. A seller was placing fruit into her bag when his spoon struck the rim of a cup, and she was suddenly aware of her father beside her. He was not there in the market. The hour had opened inside her, and she could remember the kitchen as clearly as she saw the seller’s hands.

She was sixteen again, sitting at the table in her school uniform. Her father had come home early to talk about the concert. She had prepared an argument, complete with train times and the address of the friend whose family would meet her at the station. But he had not begun with rules. He had set down his bag, filled the kettle, and asked her to show him the timetable.

She remembered doing so. She had forgotten what came next.

He studied the page as the kettle heated. He asked which train she would take home if the concert ran late, and she pointed to one marked in blue ink. He found a later train she had overlooked. He wrote its time on the back of an electricity bill, then checked whether there was enough money in the kitchen tin for both tickets.

“I don’t want you stranded,” he said.

She heard suspicion in his voice. When he asked for the friend’s telephone number, she snatched up the timetable and accused him of finding excuses to say no. He put the electricity bill down. They argued, as she had always remembered. What she had lost was the part before it: his patient work at the table, and the fact that he had been trying to find a way for her to go.

The market seller asked if she wanted a receipt. Leena said no. She carried the oranges home and stayed there until the desk clock would have shown her half an hour late.

She had gone to the concert. Her father had driven her to the station and waited while she bought her ticket. She remembered that part, too, once she let herself think about it.

For several days the office felt different to her, though none of the work had changed. She returned an hour to a retired bus driver who wanted to remember his first shift. She helped a boy find a summer afternoon at his grandmother’s house. She told a woman that the six hours she had spent asleep on a flight had never been lost; she had simply been asleep. Meanwhile, people from the council came to measure the rooms. They spoke courteously and wrote down the dimensions of each cabinet.

On the following Monday, the man in the yellow raincoat returned. This time he wore a dark sweater and carried no umbrella, though it was raining.

“I got it,” he said.

Leena invited him to sit. He remained standing.

“I remembered something while I was cleaning the bathroom. My daughter’s mother had been in labor for a long time, and they took her away. I was certain something was wrong. But what I’d forgotten was a nurse coming out to tell me she was doing well. The nurse stayed a minute because I couldn’t seem to understand her.” He looked at the floor. “I must have looked terrified.”

“Were you glad to remember?”

“Yes.” He nodded. “I was. I’d spent years thinking no one told me anything until it was over.”

After he left, Leena called the number on the council letter. She was transferred twice before reaching a woman who knew about the closure. The cabinets, she learned, would be collected by the municipal archive. Anyone could request an hour later, once the contents had been catalogued. The process might take some time.

“How much time?” Leena asked.

The woman could not say. The archive had a backlog.

That evening Leena wrote a notice for the office window. **If you have left an hour here, please come before the end of the month if you would like it returned.** Beneath it she put the address of the archive and the telephone number, though she could not promise either would help quickly.

For the first week, almost no one came. Then the local paper printed a photograph of the sign. A reporter called to ask what kind of hours people had left, and Leena refused to give examples. The next morning there was a queue past the lampshades.

She spent the day checking names and dates. The desk clock ran fast, as it often did when the room was crowded. Some visitors asked questions she could answer. Some were disappointed to learn that an hour would not bring back a person, or let them hear every word spoken long ago. A few left their envelopes in the cabinets.

One woman, looking at a small white envelope, said, “I don’t think I want this after all.”

Leena put it back without asking why.

Her brother arrived on the final Saturday with sandwiches, two of his children, and a cardboard box of pens. He had seen the notice online. While he and the children carried supplies, Leena worked through a line of people who had been waiting in the cold. By midafternoon the queue was gone.

“There are still thousands,” her brother said, looking at the cabinets.

“Yes.”

He helped her check the transfer list. Each shelf had a number; each box had to match it. The children drew pictures on scrap paper at the back table and asked if they could leave an hour from the afternoon.

“You haven’t lost it,” Leena told them.

“We might,” said the younger one.

“Then you can come and see me.”

She caught herself after she said it. Her brother looked up from the list, but neither of them corrected her.

On the last day, the clocks were as contrary as ever. Leena wrapped the travel clock in a scarf and took it home before the archive workers arrived. She checked every cabinet as they were emptied. When the shelves stood bare, she could see lighter rectangles on the walls where the boxes had shielded the paint.

The workers finished at 4:12 by the clock above the door. Leena waited while their van pulled away. Then she locked the front door and walked around the counter one last time, making sure the back window was shut and the sink tap had stopped dripping.

Outside, the shoe repairer was lowering his shutter. He asked what she would do now.

“I don’t know yet,” she said.

He nodded and wished her well. Across the street, a bus stopped. People stepped off into the evening, some hurrying toward home, others standing still for a moment to settle their bags and decide which way to go. Leena watched until the bus moved on.

Then she went home, where her father’s clock waited on the shelf. She took it down and wound it. The hands stayed at 4:17. She set it beside the bowl of oranges, put water on for tea, and called her brother to say she would visit.
